record.tranche_reason: The study steers residual-stream difference-in-means directions and measures refusal, but does not perform the original all-layer, all-position ablation.
record.gate_note: The steering section reports refusal and incoherence outcomes and directly bears on V1 and transfer to the Instruct model. The geometric results concern harmfulness subcategory directions, not refusal directions, so they are recorded under fits_no_version. AUROC and checkpoint-transfer AUROC results measure separability rather than refusal behavior and are not rows. The cited claim that harmfulness and refusal are separable is from another study, not a result of this study.
record.test_reason: The study builds harmful-minus-harmless (Alpaca) difference-in-means directions, adds them at layer 15 of Olmo 3 7B Instruct, and measures refusal rate with an LLM judge. That is a different intervention aimed at V1's causal claim. Because directions come from training checkpoints other than Instruct, it also tests transfer of the direction to the Instruct model (V6).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors treat these as harmfulness directions and use refusal only as a behavioral proxy. They conclude that late-pretraining directions steer Instruct modestly and post-training directions much more strongly. They also conclude that the positive/negative asymmetry fits harmfulness being only one input to refusal. Their headline findings also include: subcategories don't converge to one direction; in-distribution AUROC is misleading because of lexical and structural cues; and training dynamics are synchronized across subcategories.
record.recipe_differences: Uses safe-to-harmful mean activation directions and residual-stream steering, but tests steering at a fixed intermediate layer rather than ablating the direction at every layer and position.
record.method_sensitivity: Steering effectiveness depends on the source checkpoint: early directions are unreliable and often incoherent, later pretraining directions are more usable, and post-training directions produce much larger positive refusal effects. Positive and negative steering are asymmetric; normalization does not make early directions reliably control refusal.

fits_no_version.finding: Harmfulness subcategory directions stay at distinct distances from the general-harm direction and from each other across training (privacy most distinct).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Harmfulness is represented as a shared but structured multi-direction space rather than a single axis.

record.problems: Steering results are described qualitatively in the text without checkpoint- or coefficient-specific refusal rates or uncertainty estimates. Refusal is an LLM-judge proxy on a balanced prompt set, with no separate benign-prompt refusal results. The study evaluates incoherence but does not test whether other capabilities are largely preserved.
record.rows_left_out: AUROC results, including in-distribution and out-of-distribution evaluations and cross-checkpoint AUROC, were not included because they measure harmfulness separability rather than refusal behavior. Other geometric measurements were omitted because they do not measure refusal-direction geometry.

untested.parts: All-layer, all-position directional ablation; separate refusal rates on harmless prompts; capability preservation beyond incoherence.
No analysis of the multiplicity of refusal directions. Subcategory geometry concerns harmfulness, not refusal.
The authors interpret the positive/negative asymmetry as fitting harmfulness being only one input to refusal. They do not measure the two separately.
No cross-language or cross-family transfer; only checkpoint-to-Instruct within Olmo 3 7B.
Directions are only applied to Instruct. The study does not test whether a removable refusal direction exists in each checkpoint, or manipulate training.

missing.what: Per-checkpoint and per-coefficient refusal and incoherence rates for the six steering checkpoints (s1-step0, s1-step100k, s1-step900k, s2-step40k, s3-step10k, Instruct), presumably in the steering figures. The text gives only qualitative descriptions.

record.verdict_notes: The intervention is single-layer activation addition, not the original ablation. Refusal is judged on a balanced harmful/benign set with no per-group rates. There is no capability check beyond incoherence. The study is exploratory, a LessWrong post, and not peer-reviewed. Early-checkpoint rows were moved from V1 to V6, because they concern directions from other checkpoints, not Instruct's own refusal direction.

versions.untested_parts: No ablation; no intervention at every layer and position; no separate refusal rates for harmless prompts; no broad evaluation of other capabilities.
No jailbreak or attack test, and no training against ablation.
The study examines harmfulness subcategory geometry, not the geometry or multiplicity of refusal directions.
It does not separately measure harmfulness judgment and refusal decision; refusal is used as a behavioral proxy.
No transfer across languages or model variants; tested transfer is from training checkpoints to the Instruct model within the Olmo 3 7B trajectory.
The study tracks checkpoints but does not manipulate how or when refusal training occurs or test whether that causes a removable direction to exist.

source_check.notes: The pack listed no [lN] verdict ids, so l1-l4 are positional, in pack order. The text never names the six steering checkpoints, and apart from the ~31% baseline the steering results are qualitative (figures lost). There is no random-direction control for steering: the call's controls=y and uncertainty=y apply only to the AUROC section (random-label std, truthfulness contrast). Missing from the record: the asymmetry reading (harmfulness is 'only one input for refusal', citing Zhao et al.) bears on V5 but has no row, and incoherence rates were measured but not reported.

statements.correction: Olmo 3 7B Instruct, layer 15, LLM judge, balanced harmful/Alpaca-benign questions, baseline ~31%. Positive steering: 'very high, sometimes near-total'. Negative steering (coefficients -1, -1.5, -2): 'only modest reductions below baseline'. Source checkpoint not specified. No directional ablation tested.
statements.problem: The description is accurate, but the OLMo case contrasts positive addition with single-layer negative steering. The study never ablates, and it doesn't say which checkpoint the directions came from. So it doesn't show the ablation half failing in the same model.

statements.correction: lw:nKfm: LessWrong post with code. Uncertainty (std over 20 random-label runs) is reported for AUROC only; steering results have no uncertainty and no rates except the ~31% baseline. Intervention: addition/subtraction at layer 15 only. Transfer claim rests on 'directions extracted from any post-training checkpoints steer it much more effectively'.
statements.problem: The visible part (post-training directions steer Instruct strongly at layer 15) is right; the pack truncates the rest. The 'why' line credits lw:nKfm with uncertainty, but the only uncertainty in the study is the random-label AUROC std; the steering results have none. 'Activation addition and ablation' doesn't apply to lw:nKfm, which only adds or subtracts. The six steering checkpoints are never named.

statements.correction: Pretraining directions from ~s1-step100k onward: 'modest but aligned' effects. Post-training directions: much stronger. Cross-checkpoint AUROC: directions from ~s1-80k onward perform well on post-training checkpoints, and authors say final directions seem 'not to be created from scratch during alignment' (in-distribution AUROC, which they call unreliable).
statements.problem: R1/R3 are described correctly. 'Directions from s1-step100k onward steer only modestly' should be limited to pretraining directions, since post-training directions also come after s1-100k and steer strongly. Separately, the study's cross-checkpoint AUROC partly cuts against the 'weak precursors' framing.
None. 'Modest' here means pretraining directions from s1-step100k onward, and the sentence's contrast with post-training makes that clear.
